name: Mental Wellbeing Continuum
what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high to low levels. This subtopic covers what the continuum is, how it is used, and how internal and external factors influence where an individual is placed on it at any given time.
why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can define the mental wellbeing continuum and describe its key features
items.what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high levels to low levels. It is dynamic, meaning an individual's placement is not fixed and can shift over time in response to life circumstances.
items.why: This is a directly examinable definition. The word 'dynamic' and the idea that placement is not fixed are critical details that distinguish this model from categorical or diagnostic approaches.
items.example: A student who is thriving in Term 1 may shift toward the lower end of the continuum during exam period and return to the higher end after exams conclude. The same person occupies different positions on the continuum at different times.

items.title: I can describe the characteristics of each point on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: At the high end, individuals function independently, cope with daily demands without excessive distress, and regulate emotions effectively. In the middle, individuals experience temporary disruption, difficulty concentrating, and amplified emotions. At the low end, individuals show high distress, are unable to meet daily demands, and may require professional diagnosis and treatment.
items.why: Exam scenarios typically ask students to place a character on the continuum and justify their answer. Knowing the specific characteristics of each zone allows precise, evidence-based justification.
items.example: Mei Zhen coping effectively with school SACs represents the high end. Mei Zhen unable to sleep during exam period but returning to normal afterwards represents the middle. Mei Zhen developing a diagnosed anxiety disorder with panic attacks and social withdrawal represents the low end.

items.title: I can define internal factors and give examples of how they influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Internal factors are factors that arise from within the individual. They include thought patterns, genetic predisposition, and the nature of an individual's stress response. These can either protect mental wellbeing or contribute to its decline.
items.why: Internal and external factors are specifically named in the study design. Students must be able to identify, define, and distinguish them, and apply them to scenarios.
items.example: A naturally optimistic thinking style (internal factor) can protect mental wellbeing by helping a person reframe a failed assessment as a learning opportunity rather than a catastrophe.

items.title: I can define external factors and give examples of how they influence mental wellbeing
items.what: External factors are factors that arise from an individual's environment. They include loss of a significant relationship, level of education, experiences at work or school, and access to support services such as medical and psychological treatment.
items.why: External factors are equally weighted alongside internal factors in the study design. Exam responses that focus only on internal factors will be incomplete.
items.example: Mei Zhen's access to a school counsellor (external factor) helped her maintain wellbeing during exam stress. Later, access to a psychologist (external factor) supported her recovery from an anxiety disorder.

items.title: I can explain how internal and external factors interact to influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Internal and external factors do not operate independently. They interact with each other, and the combination of multiple factors can either protect mental wellbeing or lead to its decline. A protective external factor can buffer the impact of a risk-increasing internal factor.
items.why: Questions that ask students to 'explain the influence of internal and external factors' require more than listing them separately. Showing how they interact demonstrates higher-order understanding.
items.example: Mei Zhen's genetic predisposition to anxiety (internal risk factor) contributed to her developing an anxiety disorder after university. However, her strong support network and access to a psychologist (external protective factors) supported her recovery.
